newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong at 32-month high, Tokyo up slightly.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong at 32-month high, Tokyo up slightly.

text.p: Investor optimism pushed Hong Kong shares to a 32-month high on Wednesday, while in Tokyo stocks were only marginally firmer as the Dow's overnight record finish failed to inspire buyers worried by imminent elections.
Bangkok's bourse took the heaviest fall of the day, losing 2.48 percent on profit-taking, but Jakarta's composite index added 1.57 percent. Sydney was up 1.27 percent.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index closed 30.66 points or 0.26 percent higher at 11,951.88, its highest close since February 4, 1994. The blue chip index hit a 1996 intra-day high at 11,956.16.
Brokers said some investors cashed in after recent gains, but most remained bullish on the market's outlook.
"The overall market tone remains quite firm," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.
"We saw some profit-taking in the morning but it seemed to be very well absorbed and buying interest drove up the index."
He said some investors had stayed away ahead of Governor Chris Patten's annual policy speech. "There was a little bit of holding back waiting for the removal of any potential bad news."
Antony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas, said the underlying tone in the market remained "fairly strong" and he expected more gains.
Tokyo brokers said most investors were sidelined due to a lack of buying incentives despite Wall Street's rise to a record high above 5900 points at 5905.
The 225-issue Nikkei average closed 35.63 points or 0.17 percent higher at 21,498.60. Its December futures were up 10 points at 21,510.
"The U.S. market set a new record high overnight but the impact of the bullishness was limited in Tokyo," said Keiji Arai, deputy general manager at Sanyo Securities.
A general election on October 20 was subduing the market, some sources said.
"Although there is a lot of wishful speculation, we don't really know which party will win and what they will actually do to stimulate the economy," one broker said.
An analyst at Okasan Securities said the Dow's rise and the strengthening of the dollar against the yen were favourable supporting factors but were not enough to raise the average.
Thai stocks ended sharply lower as local investors sold stocks to take profits on Monday's large gains, brokers said.
The SET index closed 26.96 points, or 2.48 percent, down at 1,058.68 on moderate turnover.
"Investors sold and took profits after the market rallied sharply on Monday. They're not convinced the rally could sustain itself," said a broker.
The SET index retreated for the second day after its 4.87 percent surge on Monday in a positive reaction to Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's decision to call snap elections.
"Investors are watching political developments closely as the general elections draw closer," said Suleeyaporn Tasanasrit of UBS (East Asia) Securities.
Foreign buying of selected market heavyweights and local targeting of secondaries propelled Jakarta's composite index to close at the day-high of 589.31 points, up 9.10 points.
Australian shares stormed to their highest close in five months on a flood of afternoon buying interest inspired by surging share price index futures.
The All Ordinaries index jumped 29.1 points to 2,314.6.
Malaysia's benchmark composite index was up 4.36 or 0.38 percent at 1139.32.
At 1132 GMT, the dollar traded at 111.80/1.90 yen and 1.5255/60 marks.
SIMEX Brent futures prices were firmer in late dealings, with worries about low products inventories driving prices.
November Brent last traded on SIMEX at $23.26 per barrel, up 19 cents from London's close.
Hong Kong bullion ended at US$379.00/50 an ounce against New York's US$378.70/379.20 close on Monday.
